plimsoll trainer · 08 / broker transports

The API broker

Code you do not trust needs to read from your API, and your API needs a key. Everything about the broker follows from one decision: the key never enters the room with the code. The code asks for a route; a guard on the host side checks it against a short list, attaches the key, and forwards it. A fully compromised run holds nothing worth stealing.

01

The line the key never crosses

The room has no network. One private line leads out of it to the broker, which holds the profile's route list and the credential minted for this run. The room changes with the provider; the guard does not.

The room

02

The route check, exactly

The broker approves a string only if it is byte for byte the string that will be sent. Type a path, or tap one of the attempts, and read the verdict the broker would give against this profile's list. The rules below are the daemon's, in the same order.

The profile's Allow listGET /v1/warehouses
GET /v1/items/*
GET /v1/items/*/stock
POST /v1/orders

Why the string has to match the wire. A guest could write /v1/items/%2e%2e/admin: the broker would see a harmless-looking segment, and the upstream would decode it to ... Or /v1/items/42?x=/stock: the list would match it against a longer template while the request actually hits the shorter route, because net/http strips everything after the ?. So anything that is not already in decoded, canonical, wire-ready form is refused before matching, and the string approved is the string sent. The template that matched, never the path, is what the call trace records.

03

The eight words

Everything on this page is these eight ideas moving around.

sandboxa room where code we do not trust runs.The provider decides how thick its walls are: in-process, a container, a container with gVisor, a microVM.
granta per-run permission slip: this one run may call these routes on this one API.Off by default, twice: no grant means no network, and an empty route list reaches nothing.
profilea named grant held by the daemon.Origin, routes, allowed callers, scopes, how the credential is minted. A caller selects one by name and can change nothing in it.
brokerthe guard on the host side of the line.Checks the route, counts the budget, attaches the key, forwards, records the template.
credentialwhat the guard attaches.A fresh short-lived JWT per run with the caller as its subject, or one server-held static bearer. Either way it lives in Go.
the linethe one way out of the room.A Unix socket, a host function, or one allowed exit. Only request and response bytes cross it.
egresstraffic leaving the room.Denied. The line is not egress: it goes to the guard, not to the internet.
forward proxythe industry's name for the guard.A mandatory exit every outbound call must pass through, holding the policy. Service meshes do this with an egress gateway.

04

Four numbers the guard counts

Generous for honest code and fatal for a loop that has run away, which is the only thing a per-run cap can usefully tell apart.

256 callsper run, by defaultA profile whose workload is a loop by design raises max_calls, never past 100,000.
1 MiBrequest bodyRead from the guest and counted before any matching.
4 MiBresponse bodyA larger upstream answer keeps its row, marked undelivered, so a capped 200 is not a success.
256 rowscall traceWhatever the call budget. Calls past the cap count as dropped, and a finding says "at least".

05

E2B: the room is on someone else's servers

With docker the room is on the host, so a socket reaches under the door. A microVM runs on E2B's infrastructure; there is no hallway to run a line down. The rule does not change, so the plumbing has to.

  1. All egress denied. The VM's network is off, and the startup smoke test creates a no-grant VM and proves it live. That is the deny-all floor.
  2. One allowed exit. Pointed at plimsoll's host-side guard, the URL in E2B_GUARD_URL. The guard delegates to the same broker as every other provider.
  3. The guest cannot forge the exit. E2B's per-host header transform attaches the run's guard token to requests on their way out, outside the guest, so the code inside never sees it and cannot mint its own. The guard authenticates and admits a request before reading its body.
  4. No guard, no grant. With E2B_GUARD_URL unset, an E2B grant is refused outright rather than downgraded to something weaker.
  5. The exception is proved separately. The smoke test proves deny-all, not "denied except for the guard". make e2b-guard-live proves the guarded path, and it fails rather than skips when unconfigured, so a pass can only come from having exercised it.

06

The mainstream pattern, with one rule made stricter

Mediating outbound calls from code you do not fully trust is a solved problem. plimsoll uses the standard shapes, and refuses the one the cloud uses for its own VMs.

Forced-egress forward proxy

Default-deny network; every outbound call must pass one proxy that holds the policy. Envoy, Istio and Linkerd egress gateways are this shape. The guard is exactly this.

Short-lived scoped tokens

A broker vends a narrow, expiring credential and injects it at the proxy. SPIFFE and SPIRE, OAuth client credentials. The JWT profile is this, with the calling principal as the subject.

Metadata server: refused

A link-local endpoint hands the credential into the VM, the way AWS IMDS and the GCP metadata server do, which is why IMDSv2 had to add defences against code inside the VM asking for it. For hostile code the key must never enter the room, so this shape is out.

The route checker applies the broker's published matching rules in the page; it is a model of the daemon's check, not a call to it, and the path you type never leaves your browser. Every limit and identifier here is checked against the daemon's source by the tests in this directory.
